lines.text: The largest country on Earth, shaped by princes, khans, tsars and commissars. This is the story of Russia, from Kievan Rus to the war in Ukraine.
Long before any people, a rift in Siberia opened Lake Baikal, the deepest and oldest lake in the world, holding a fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh water.
The story of the Russian state begins in Kyiv, where princes bound Slavic lands together. Around 988 their ruler Vladimir took Orthodox Christianity.
In 1147 a small settlement named Moscow first appears in the records. One day it would rule an empire.
A few years later a wooden fort rose on the hill above the river, the first Kremlin, which would grow into the seat of Russia's rulers.
Then the Mongols came. From the 1240s the Golden Horde ruled the steppes, and Russian princes paid it tribute for generations.
Under the Horde, the principality of Moscow began its slow rise, the seed of the country we call Russia.
Its grand dukes gathered the Russian lands one by one, and in 1480 they finally threw off the Horde.
Ivan the Fourth, remembered as the Terrible, became the first to be crowned tsar. He conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, then ruled with growing cruelty.
To mark his victories, Saint Basil's Cathedral rose on Red Square, crowned with its many-coloured onion domes.
After years of turmoil, in 1613 Michael Romanov took the throne, founding a dynasty that would reign for three centuries.
His grandson Peter the Great toured Europe to learn its ways, then built a navy, remade the army, and defeated Sweden.
In 1703 Peter founded a new city on the Baltic marshes, Saint Petersburg, his window on Europe and soon the capital.
In 1721 he proclaimed the Russian Empire, which would stretch across Siberia and into Central Asia.
Catherine the Great, born a German princess, seized the throne in 1762, pushed the empire to the Black Sea, and wrote to the thinkers of France.
Her art collection in the Winter Palace became the Hermitage, today one of the largest museums in the world.
In Moscow, the Bolshoi Theatre was founded, home to Russian ballet and opera ever since.
In 1799 Alexander Pushkin was born, the poet of Eugene Onegin and the founder of modern Russian literature.
In 1812 Napoleon marched on Moscow. Russia retreated and burned what it left behind, and the winter destroyed his great army.
Fyodor Dostoevsky, once sentenced to death and then spared, would write Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.
Leo Tolstoy would write War and Peace and Anna Karenina, and his ideas on nonviolence would later inspire Gandhi.
The chemist Dmitri Mendeleev would set out the periodic table, leaving gaps for elements no one had yet found.
And Tchaikovsky would give the world Swan Lake, The Nutcracker and the 1812 Overture.
In 1861 Tsar Alexander the Second freed the serfs, tens of millions of peasants, though many stayed poor, paying for their land.
In 1870 Vladimir Lenin was born, the revolutionary who would bring the Bolsheviks to power.
Joseph Stalin, born in Georgia, would rule the Soviet Union through terror and forced industry for a quarter of a century.
By the early nineteen hundreds the Trans-Siberian Railway linked Moscow with the Pacific, the longest line in the world.
In 1905, after Bloody Sunday, strikes and mutinies swept the empire, and the tsar had to grant an elected Duma.
In 1917 revolution came in earnest. Nicholas the Second gave up the throne, and by the autumn Lenin's Bolsheviks held power.
After a bitter civil war, in 1922 the Soviet Union was founded, a communist state of many republics.
From 1930 its labour camps, the Gulag, held millions of prisoners across the frozen north and east.
Boris Yeltsin, born in 1931, would become the first president of the Russian Federation.
Mikhail Gorbachev, born that same year, would be the last Soviet leader, opening up society with glasnost and perestroika.
And Yuri Gagarin, born in 1934, would be the first human to fly in space.
In 1941 Germany invaded, and Leningrad was besieged for almost nine hundred days. About a million people died.
On the Volga, the Red Army held Stalingrad and trapped a whole German army, a turning point of the war in Europe.
In 1952, in Leningrad, Vladimir Putin was born, a future intelligence officer who would lead Russia from 1999.
From the mid fifties the Soviet space program raced ahead, with the first satellite, the first man and the first woman in space.
In October 1957 Sputnik began to circle the Earth, beeping its signal to a startled world.
In April 1961 Vostok 1 carried Gagarin once around the planet, in under two hours.
In 1976 Alexei Navalny was born, the opposition leader who would expose corruption at the top, and die in an Arctic prison.
In 1986 the space station Mir was launched, home to crews from many countries for fifteen years.
In 1991, after a failed coup, the republics broke away, and at the end of December the Soviet Union ceased to exist.
Russia, now under Yeltsin, went to war against breakaway Chechnya in 1994.
In 2018 Russia hosted the World Cup, and France won the final in Moscow.
In February 2022, eight years after seizing Crimea, Russia launched a full invasion of Ukraine, a war that has killed many and driven millions from home.
From Kyiv's princes to the Kremlin today, Russia's story is still unfolding.
